The results could help researchers develop further testing to predict a patient’s risk of metastasis and support more personalized […]

item.description: NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope has painted a vibrant tapestry of the legendary supernova remnant Cassiopeia A (Cas A). Remnants like these are the clouds of gas and dust that remain following the explosion of a massive star and will eventually seed a new generation of stars and planets. This high-resolution, mid-infrared observation from Webb […]

item.title: New gum disease treatment kills bad bacteria while sparing the good
item.description: Researchers in Japan have developed an innovative gum disease treatment that uses egg yolk antibodies and near-infrared light to destroy harmful bacteria without harming beneficial microbes. Unlike conventional treatments, the approach preserves the mouth's natural bacterial balance and protects healthy gum cells. In mice, it significantly reduced the bone loss associated with periodontitis, a major cause of tooth loss.

item.title: A galactic shock wave could rewrite the map of the Milky Way
item.description: A surprising discovery suggests the Milky Way may be making stars in places where most galaxies cannot. Scientists found evidence that a massive rotating structure near the galactic center is creating powerful shock waves that trigger star formation rather than suppress it. Even more unexpectedly, part of the Norma spiral arm may not be a spiral arm at all, but a vast region where new stars are being born.

item.title: Two monster black holes from the dawn of time defy explanation
item.description: Astronomers have discovered the oldest known compact pair of quasars, powered by two enormous black holes that existed just 900 million years after the Big Bang. Weighing an astonishing 1.5 billion and 400 million times the mass of the Sun, these cosmic giants somehow grew to incredible sizes far earlier than current theories can explain.

item.title: Mysterious new viruses reveal a missing link in evolution
item.description: Scientists have discovered previously unknown viruses that could help explain how some of life’s earliest biological structures evolved. The surprising findings challenge a longstanding evolutionary theory and suggest that viruses may have hidden capabilities far beyond simply infecting cells.

item.title: Scientists discover that leukemia can begin developing 50 years before diagnosis
item.description: A groundbreaking study reveals that acute myeloid leukemia (AML), an aggressive blood cancer, can begin developing more than 50 years before diagnosis, with the first cancer-driving mutation appearing before age 20 in two-thirds of cases. Scientists discovered that these mutated cells grow in surprisingly predictable patterns, accelerating dramatically as additional mutations accumulate.

item.title: Archaeologists reveal a powerful Iron Age king may have been a woman
item.description: Archaeologists have uncovered evidence that Verica, the Iron Age ruler whose exile helped trigger Rome’s invasion of Britain in AD 43, was actually a woman. The discovery challenges centuries of historical assumptions and suggests that a largely forgotten female leader may have changed the course of British history.

item.title: Laser Focus at the Top of the World
item.description: A next-generation geodetic instrument developed by NASA, part of a network that helps measure satellites’ orbits and the planet’s shape, has debuted in Svalbard, Norway.

item.title: This tiny spider named after Stephen Colbert has a genome 50% larger than a human’s
item.description: A tiny California trapdoor spider named after Stephen Colbert has a genome roughly 50% larger than a human's, despite being only about the size of a quarter. Scientists discovered that its enormous genome contains 4.6 billion DNA base pairs and 52 chromosomes, revealing surprising clues about spider evolution.

item.title: Mice slept 70% less after scientists switched off these brain cells
item.description: Scientists have discovered brain cells that actively generate the irresistible urge to sleep, and shutting them down allowed mice to sleep 70% less than normal. Remarkably, many of the animals avoided the severe behavioral consequences of sleep deprivation, raising intriguing possibilities for future sleep research.

item.title: U.S. loses measles elimination status after 25 years as vaccine myths persist
item.description: The United States has lost its measles elimination status after more than 25 years, and a new survey reveals widespread misconceptions about the deadly disease and its vaccine. With measles cases surging, more than one-third of Americans still believe or are uncertain about the debunked vaccine-autism link, while most don't know the disease's risks or how many vaccine doses children need.

item.title: Scientists discover a surprising link between weak bones and faster brain aging
item.description: Weakening bones may reveal more about brain health than scientists previously realized, with new research linking lower spinal bone density to faster cognitive decline and accelerated changes in the brain's white matter. The surprising connection suggests that routine medical scans could help uncover hidden warning signs of brain aging and identify people at increased risk of dementia.

item.title: Common medications may secretly rewire your gut, with effects lasting for years
item.description: Medications taken years or even long ago may leave lasting changes in your gut microbiome, according to a study of more than 2,500 people. Researchers discovered that common drugs, including antidepressants, blood pressure medications, and anxiety treatments, can leave microbial “fingerprints” long after patients stop taking them. Surprisingly, some anxiety medications had effects comparable to broad-spectrum antibiotics.

item.title: Type 2 diabetes linked to 53% higher Alzheimer’s risk, major review finds
item.description: People with type 2 diabetes face a 53% higher risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease, according to a major new review of 40 studies. Researchers estimate that nearly five out of every 1,000 people with type 2 diabetes develop Alzheimer’s each year. By focusing specifically on these two conditions, the study offers a clearer understanding of a potentially serious connection between metabolic health and brain health.

item.title: 65 Years of Human Spaceflight at NASA Johnson
item.description: For 65 years, NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston has helped shape human spaceflight, from the Gemini missions that demonstrated rendezvous and docking techniques needed for Apollo to the research conducted aboard the International Space Station, which has supported a continuous human presence for more than 26 years. Today, Johnson teams are preparing crews and […]

item.title: Interstellar solar sails hit a bizarre problem at 75% of light speed
item.description: Scientists have discovered a surprising obstacle to interstellar travel: at extreme speeds, the light propelling futuristic solar sails could actually begin slowing them down. Once a spacecraft reaches 75% of the speed of light, some scattered light starts producing drag, potentially complicating humanity’s plans to reach distant stars.

item.title: A mysterious gap hints at black holes born from stars that never exploded
item.description: Massive stars may be quietly collapsing into black holes without ever producing the spectacular supernova explosions scientists typically expect. A surprising pattern in 257 black hole mergers suggests these mysterious stellar disappearances could explain the origins of a large population of black holes throughout the universe.

item.title: DNA’s secret sunscreen may have helped life survive on early Earth
item.description: Scientists have uncovered a surprising reason why early life may have survived Earth's intense ultraviolet radiation: a key component of DNA appears to turn potentially destructive damage into something easier to repair. The discovery could help solve a decades-old evolutionary mystery and reveal how life endured the harsh conditions of our planet's earliest days.

item.title: A 194-year-old tortoise has a remarkable anti-aging secret hidden in its DNA
item.description: At an astonishing 194 years old, Jonathan the giant tortoise is the world's oldest living land animal, and scientists may have finally uncovered the secrets behind his extraordinary lifespan. Researchers identified 287 unique genetic variants linked to processes that help repair damaged DNA, control inflammation, regulate insulin, and suppress cancer.

item.title: Scientists discover a hidden eye disease that slowly steals night vision
item.description: Scientists have discovered a new genetic eye disease that can silently damage peripheral and night vision while leaving central sight largely unaffected for years. The condition may be detectable through an unusual difficulty adjusting to darkness, offering a potential early warning sign before irreversible retinal damage occurs.

item.title: AI uncovers hidden bladder cancer warning signs years before diagnosis
item.description: Scientists have developed an AI tool that can uncover hidden warning signs of bladder cancer up to five years before diagnosis, identifying 85% of cases in a major study involving nearly 70,000 patients. By revealing subtle patterns that conventional screening misses, the technology could help doctors detect cancer earlier and spare patients unnecessary invasive procedures.

item.title: Alzheimer’s breakthrough exposes a hidden flaw in the brain’s cleanup system
item.description: Scientists have identified a gene that helps the brain’s immune cells contain harmful plaques linked to Alzheimer’s, potentially revealing a new way to fight the disease. When the gene malfunctioned in mice, toxic buildup accelerated and cognitive abilities declined, raising hopes that restoring its function could help protect the brain.

item.title: A common blood pressure drug has a surprising effect on calorie-burning brown fat
item.description: Scientists have discovered that a common blood pressure drug can activate calorie-burning brown fat in mice, potentially opening a new path toward improving metabolic health. An analysis of more than 100,000 patients also revealed surprising links between brown fat and lower rates of heart disease, diabetes, anxiety, and depression.

item.title: AI may not work like the human brain after all, scientists discover
item.description: AI may not think like the human brain after all, according to a striking new discovery that challenges how scientists understand artificial intelligence. Researchers found that even AI models that closely predict brain activity may rely on internal processes the brain doesn't use, raising important questions about their reliability in neuroscience research.

item.title: Time may be far stranger than we realize. Scientists have a way to test it
item.description: Time may be far stranger than we realize, and scientists have proposed a way to detect clocks experiencing multiple flows of time simultaneously. Using atomic clocks with dramatically enhanced sensitivity, researchers hope to reveal a never-before-observed quantum effect that could transform our understanding of time and gravity.

item.title: A giant star swallowed another star. James Webb reveals the aftermath
item.description: Astronomers have witnessed a spectacular cosmic collision in the Andromeda galaxy, where a small star spiraled into a giant star 18,000 times brighter than the Sun, triggering a violent eruption. NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope captured the aftermath just 47 days later, revealing new details about how two stars can merge into one.

item.title: Who was buried in Westminster Abbey's Roman coffin? A 150-year mystery may be solved
item.description: A mysterious skeleton discovered in a Roman sarcophagus at Westminster Abbey may finally be identified after more than 150 years. New dating evidence suggests the remains belonged to a high-ranking medieval abbot who was buried inside a centuries-old recycled Roman coffin.

item.title: A 50-year-old theory about evolution may have been wrong all along
item.description: A decades-old theory suggesting that evolution protects its most important genes from mutations has been dealt a major blow. An extensive new analysis of mutations in bacteria and yeast found no evidence that essential genes mutate less frequently than other genes. Researchers say earlier studies may have been misled by harmful mutations that disappeared through natural selection before scientists could detect them.

item.title: Even scientists can't agree on what science actually is
item.description: Scientists cannot agree on what science actually is, and a new study finds their views are surprisingly more divided than those of the general public. The findings could help explain public frustration with scientific uncertainty and raise questions about how artificial intelligence might reshape future discoveries.

item.title: Scientists say the human family tree may need a radical rewrite
item.description: The human family tree may need a major overhaul. New research from Monash University challenges the traditional classification of our ancient ancestors, arguing that species such as Australopithecus and Paranthropus should be grouped within our own genus, Homo. As scientists uncover more fossils and analyze evolutionary relationships, the boundaries that once separated these ancient relatives are becoming increasingly difficult to defend.

item.title: Microplastics may be more dangerous than we thought. Scientists just discovered why
item.description: Microplastics may be doing something far more dangerous than simply accumulating in our bodies. Scientists have discovered that tiny plastic particles can interact with water to generate highly reactive molecules capable of damaging cells and tissues. This unexpected chemical activity could help explain growing evidence linking microplastic exposure to serious health problems, including heart attacks, strokes, and neurological disorders.

item.title: After 8 years in space, a groundbreaking X-ray telescope finally opens its eyes
item.description: After eight years and 10 billion kilometers in space, a groundbreaking X-ray telescope heading to Mercury has captured its first cosmic observations and is performing even better than scientists expected. The instrument could soon reveal Mercury's hidden chemical secrets and transform our understanding of how the solar system's smallest planet formed.

item.title: A decades-old mystery about light could hold the key to faster internet
item.description: A promising material for ultra-fast optical communications has held a secret for decades, but scientists may have finally cracked it. Researchers at KAIST and Caltech have precisely measured how barium titanate controls and absorbs light, resolving longstanding uncertainties that have slowed its development. Their findings could make it easier to build optical devices that transmit information faster while wasting less light.

item.title: BepiColombo finally reaches Mercury after eight-year odyssey
item.description: Nature, Published online: 21 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03803-8 European and Japanese probes will trace different paths around the planet to study its surface and its surroundings.

item.title: Einstein’s relativity just upended a fundamental rule of chemistry
item.description: A surprising discovery at Brown University is challenging one of chemistry's most fundamental textbook explanations. Researchers found direct evidence that Einstein's theory of relativity changes how heavy atoms form triple bonds, causing normally distinct types of chemical bonds to blend together. The breakthrough confirms a decades-old prediction and suggests that traditional chemistry rules don't fully apply to heavy elements such as bismuth.

item.title: NASA’s Voyager 1 is now so far away that light takes 24 hours to reach it
item.description: NASA’s Voyager 1 has reached an extraordinary milestone, traveling 16.1 billion miles from Earth to become the first spacecraft so distant that its signals take a full day to reach us. Nearly 50 years after launch, the aging probe continues its historic journey through interstellar space, pushing the limits of human exploration despite dwindling power and technical challenges.

item.title: NASA's powerful Moon rocket engine roars through a dramatic 200-second test
item.description: NASA has successfully tested a powerful RS-25 rocket engine, firing it for 200 seconds to gather data that could make future Moon missions safer and more reliable. The test supports preparations for the 2028 Artemis IV Moon landing and NASA’s ultimate ambition of sending astronauts to Mars.

item.title: Keto diet slashes liver fat by 67% in just 4 months
item.description: A new clinical trial found that the ketogenic diet dramatically outperformed Mediterranean and low-fat diets in reducing liver fat and improving metabolic health, even when participants lost similar amounts of weight. After just four to five months, about half of those following keto no longer met the criteria for prediabetes, while their liver fat dropped by an average of 67%.

item.title: Scientists turn Moon dust into LEGO-like bricks for future lunar bases
item.description: Scientists have found a way to 3D-print Moon dust into LEGO-like bricks, raising the possibility of building lunar bases using materials already on the Moon. The experimental blocks still need to be strengthened, but the technology could transform how humans construct permanent settlements beyond Earth.

item.title: CERN scientists finally find evidence of a particle decay so rare it took 40 years to detect
item.description: Scientists at CERN have found the first evidence of an incredibly rare particle decay after more than 40 years of searching, detecting a process expected to occur just once in every 10 billion beauty particles. The breakthrough could help physicists explore a mysterious microscopic realm where unknown particles and forces may be hiding.

item.title: This simple habit is linked to a 33% lower risk of Alzheimer's
item.description: Reading for pleasure may have surprisingly powerful benefits for the brain, with studies linking it to better memory, reduced stress, improved mental health, and a lower risk of dementia. Researchers highlight findings that just five minutes of fiction can reduce stress by up to 20%, while reading has also been associated with a 33% lower risk of Alzheimer's disease.

item.title: For better mental health, how often you exercise may matter more than how hard
item.description: A study of more than 10,000 college students found that exercising regularly may be more important for mental health than pushing yourself through intense or lengthy workouts. Students who exercised less frequently were more likely to experience depression and anxiety a year later, suggesting that consistency could be a key ingredient in protecting mental well-being.

item.title: Two massive stars may be secretly feeding the Milky Way’s supermassive black hole
item.description: Astronomers have traced mysterious gas clouds near the Milky Way's central supermassive black hole to a massive pair of stars whose colliding winds appear to create dense clumps of material. These clouds may eventually feed the black hole, revealing a surprising connection between stellar activity and the growth of cosmic giants.

item.title: Powerful new weight-loss drug helps patients cut knee pain in half
item.description: A powerful experimental weight-loss drug helped people with knee osteoarthritis lose about 25% of their body weight at the highest dose, while roughly two-thirds experienced at least a 50% reduction in knee pain. The findings suggest retatrutide could transform treatment for millions suffering from painful arthritis, although its ability to prevent further joint damage remains unknown.

item.title: A 3-million-year-old child just made human evolution far more complicated
item.description: A groundbreaking study of the 3-million-year-old Taung Child fossil suggests that several ancient human ancestors once thought to belong to the same species may actually represent different branches of our evolutionary family tree. The discovery challenges a century of assumptions and reveals how dramatic climate changes helped shape a surprisingly complex story of human origins.

item.title: A study of 30,000 people reveals which antidepressants may work best
item.description: A major review involving more than 30,000 people found that three antidepressants, including Lexapro and Cymbalta, may be more effective than Prozac at maintaining improvements in depression symptoms. However, limitations in the research and a lack of truly long-term data mean scientists still cannot say which antidepressant is best.

item.title: Experimental compound burns fat without sacrificing muscle
item.description: Researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a compound that could transform weight-loss treatment by helping the body burn more energy instead of suppressing appetite like Ozempic and Wegovy. In mice, the compound boosted energy expenditure by up to 18%, improved blood sugar control, reduced liver fat, and promoted weight loss without significant muscle loss. Even more promising, combining it with existing GLP-1 medications produced greater benefits than either treatment alone.

item.title: Scientists tested 212 plant-based foods. Every single one contained fungal toxins
item.description: A new study has uncovered a surprising concern hiding in popular plant-based foods and drinks. Researchers tested 212 vegan and vegetarian products sold in the UK, including meat alternatives, oat milk, almond milk, and soy milk, and found that every single one contained at least one potentially harmful fungal toxin. Known as mycotoxins, these naturally occurring compounds can contaminate grains, legumes, and seeds during farming and storage.

item.title: This 6-million-year-old whale may have had the most crooked face in mammal history
item.description: A bizarre whale that lived roughly 6 million years ago had a face so dramatically crooked that scientists believe it may have been the most asymmetrical of any mammal. Discovered in Peru, the extinct pygmy sperm whale Scaphokogia huachafo had an enormous downward-curving snout and a skull so distorted that researchers initially thought it had been damaged after death. Instead, its strange anatomy appears to have been an extraordinary evolutionary adaptation for hunting along the seafloor.

item.title: Something strange is living beneath the skin of deep-sea pigs
item.description: Scientists have discovered a strange bacterium hiding beneath the skin of deep-sea creatures known as sea pigs, revealing an unexpected biological partnership. The microbe has an unusually tiny genome, yet more than a quarter of its DNA is devoted to making surface proteins, some of them exceptionally large. Researchers suspect it depends heavily on its host for survival, but what the sea pigs gain in return remains a mystery.

item.title: Why hydrogen flames can glow orange, then turn nearly invisible
item.description: Hydrogen flames can shift from bright orange to nearly invisible depending on something unexpected: tiny amounts of sodium floating in the air. Scientists say this discovery could help make future hydrogen-powered stoves and ovens safer by replacing visual flame detection with specialized sensors.

item.title: Antarctica’s ice cliffs are collapsing faster than expected, but there’s a twist
item.description: A surprising new study suggests Antarctica's towering ice cliffs may be less vulnerable to catastrophic collapse than scientists once feared. After tracking more than 15,000 ice cliffs, researchers discovered that even the tallest cliffs, which can collapse at alarming speeds, often stabilize rather than triggering an unstoppable chain reaction. Underwater ridges, surrounding water, and broken ice appear to provide natural defenses against further collapse.

item.title: Why don't weight-loss drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy work for everyone?
item.description: Why do Ozempic and Wegovy produce dramatic weight loss for some people but disappointing results for others? Scientists are investigating whether the body's hidden energy-saving response could help explain the difference and unlock more effective, personalized weight-loss treatments.

item.title: Stonehenge’s six-ton mystery deepens as scientists narrow their search
item.description: A major new investigation into Stonehenge’s mysterious six-ton Altar Stone has uncovered fresh clues while ruling out several suspected sources. Once thought to have originated in Wales, the massive sandstone slab is now believed to have come from northeastern Scotland, although researchers have yet to find an exact match.

item.title: Scientists discover a hidden hereditary form of aggressive prostate cancer
item.description: Scientists have discovered a rare inherited mutation in the CDK12 gene linked to aggressive prostate cancer, with all five identified carriers developing metastatic disease between ages 44 and 62. The finding could lead to expanded genetic testing, helping families uncover hidden cancer risks and potentially detect the disease while it is still treatable.

item.title: Is free will an illusion? New brain research reveals a surprising twist
item.description: New research reveals that the brain makes free choices and forced decisions using surprisingly similar neural processes, with activity building toward a decision before we act. The discovery challenges assumptions about free will while suggesting that our personal preferences and experiences still shape what we choose.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 19 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03748-y Climate change is creating conditions that pump up the intensity of hurricanes and typhoons just as the storms reach the coast.

item.title: People entering old age now have better memory than their parents did
item.description: Nature, Published online: 19 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03783-9 Older people today maintain memory function for longer than previous generations did, according to a study of 219,000 adults.

item.title: University students are biggest spreaders of COVID
item.description: Nature, Published online: 19 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03746-0 Undergraduates were the first group to spread genetic variants of SARS-CoV-2 during the pandemic, mega-analysis finds.

item.title: Sore throat? The brain has surprising control over how ill you feel
item.description: Nature, Published online: 19 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03774-w The brain might decode pathogens, store memories of previous illnesses and prepare the body for future threats.

item.title: AI is ditching hallucinated references — and other bad habits
item.description: Nature, Published online: 19 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03753-1 An analysis finds that many undesirable LLM behaviours dissipate after about 16 months.

item.title: What do various cancers have in common?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 19 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03379-3 An analysis of 42 cancer types reveals shared patterns of gene activity in the tumour microenvironment, which might point to treatments that work across a range of cancers.

item.title: Author Correction: Pharmacological inhibition of METTL1 as a therapy against solid and blood cancers
item.description: Nature, Published online: 19 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11421-7 Author Correction: Pharmacological inhibition of METTL1 as a therapy against solid and blood cancers

item.title: Author Correction: Replication-stress-induced chromatin loops protect fork stability
item.description: Nature, Published online: 19 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11436-0 Author Correction: Replication-stress-induced chromatin loops protect fork stability

item.title: AI is turbocharging cyberattacks — can computer scientists catch up?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 19 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03775-9 Cybersecurity researchers who don’t use the technology for spotting software bugs now 'risk falling behind'.

item.title: Daily briefing: Homo erectus had what it takes to thrive in the rainforest
item.description: Nature, Published online: 19 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03797-3 Fossil teeth suggest that Homo erectus could live in a habitat researchers thought that only Homo sapiens could hack. Plus, what experts think remains underappreciated in neuroscience and tips on networking at a conference.

item.title: Bacteria and viruses team up to hasten the demise of algal blooms
item.description: Nature, Published online: 19 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03606-x Algal blooms are important ecological phenomena that drive carbon fixation and fuel the marine food web. Viral infection often ends them abruptly. Some bacteria can sense infected algal cells and then act in synergy with viruses to expedite a bloom’s collapse.

item.title: Anthropic IPO: four ways the AI giant wants to disrupt science
item.description: Nature, Published online: 19 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03788-4 The firm aims to cure diseases, accelerate discovery and automate science — but many researchers are sceptical of its lofty ambitions.

item.title: This strange creature lived 309 million years ago, long before the dinosaurs
item.description: More than 300 million years ago, long before dinosaurs roamed Earth, the Chicago area was a steamy, swampy landscape teeming with bizarre creatures. Now, scientists at the Field Museum have identified a previously unrecognized species of ancient amphibian ancestor, revealing new clues about the evolution of frogs and salamanders.

item.title: Too much exercise could leave your brain stuck in overdrive
item.description: Exercising too much without adequate recovery may disrupt brain chemistry in surprising ways. Scientists found that mice subjected to prolonged, intense training had elevated dopamine levels in a brain region linked to memory and emotions, even 48 hours after exercising. The discovery could help explain why overtrained athletes sometimes struggle with insomnia, anxiety, and persistent fatigue, although these symptoms were not directly measured.

item.title: A rare disease reveals a hidden flaw in the immune system
item.description: Scientists have discovered that a rare, potentially life-threatening inflammatory disorder is driven by malfunctioning immune cells, overturning three decades of scientific understanding. The breakthrough points to a promising new treatment using existing medications, with one severely affected infant already showing substantial improvement.

item.title: Scientists create a remarkable new rechargeable battery using vitamin B12
item.description: Scientists have found a surprising new use for vitamin B12, developing a rechargeable battery that uses the essential nutrient to help generate and store electricity. The prototype survived up to 250 charging cycles and could open the door to safer, cheaper, and more environmentally friendly alternatives to lithium-ion batteries.

item.title: Why do farts smell so bad? The secret is brewing in your gut
item.description: The secret behind truly terrible-smelling farts lies in tiny amounts of sulfur-containing gases produced by gut bacteria as they digest food. Scientists reveal why some foods make farts smell worse, why loud farts aren't always the stinkiest, and how our noses evolved to detect these powerful odors.

item.title: Bizarre deep-sea fish with a see-through head captured in stunning 4K
item.description: Deep-sea researchers have captured stunning new footage of an extraordinarily rare fish with a transparent head and rotating eyes nearly 2,000 feet beneath the ocean's surface. Known as the barreleye fish, this bizarre creature uses its upward-pointing eyes to spot prey before rotating them forward to track its next meal, all while a transparent dome protects them.

item.title: NASA pushes Mars helicopter blades beyond the speed of sound
item.description: NASA has successfully tested Mars helicopter rotor blades at supersonic speeds, boosting potential lift by 30% and overcoming a major obstacle to more powerful aircraft on the Red Planet. The breakthrough could enable next-generation helicopters to carry heavier scientific equipment, fly farther, and explore places beyond the reach of traditional rovers.

item.title: Conference networking made simple, in three short videos
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03678-9 Working the room is a skill you can practise and prepare for. Here’s how.

item.title: First observation of a giant star swallowing its neighbour
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03784-8 Finding provides new insights into what happens within stellar mergers — plus, using quantum physics to securely pinpoint someone’s location.

item.title: How to make AI data centres more sustainable
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03708-6 Tech companies and governments face opposition over data centres’ expansion, in part because of their huge power requirements. They must not be powered with fossil fuels.

item.title: Microbiome home tests are taking off. Can they be trusted?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03710-y Our reporter mailed off her poo to find out what two companies say about her microbiome. Here’s what she found.

item.title: Tropical land-use intensification reshapes biodiversity in expected and unexpected ways
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03602-1 Global agricultural demand has increased over the past few decades, driving land-use intensification in some of the world’s most biodiverse regions. An assessment of some 40,000 species, from soil microorganisms to vertebrates, in Sumatra, Indonesia, reveals that agricultural intensification threatens biodiversity through species loss and changes in community composition across different spatial scales.

item.title: Kings of the jungle? This early human had surprising survival skills that rivalled ours
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03777-7 Teeth found in south China challenge the idea that Homo erectus lived only in woodlands and on savannahs.

item.title: Daily briefing: Can you spot the ‘tortured phrases’?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03791-9 Take Nature’s quiz to test your skills as a research-integrity sleuth. Plus, a milestone for Voyager 1 and the United States has lost its measles elimination status.

item.title: Intra-stellar: a star inside a giant star
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03273-y Long-term monitoring of a giant star in the Andromeda galaxy reveals, for the first time, the decay of the orbit of another star inside the giant’s envelope.

item.title: Glucose-powered implant brings devices for treating diabetes a step closer
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03377-5 A device that stimulates the main nerve between the brain and the internal organs when blood sugar is high is an effective therapy in rat models of diabetes.

item.title: Band-Edge-Extended Heterointerfaces for Perovskite Solar Cells and Tandems
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11427-1 Band-Edge-Extended Heterointerfaces for Perovskite Solar Cells and Tandems

item.title: Poxviruses probably evolved in the digestive system of animals
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03436-x Large and giant DNA viruses that infect unicellular eukaryotes are abundant in the environment but have rarely been found in the gut microbiome. The discovery of such viruses that prevail in the digestive system of humans and animals exposes a long-overlooked facet of the gut microbiome that clarifies the origin of poxviruses.

item.title: Meet ‘egoviruses’: the surprise microbes living in the guts of millions of people
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03766-w Egoviruses could be the evolutionary missing link between giant viruses that infect single-celled organisms and those that can infect people.

item.title: A new view of Amazonian leaf seasonality
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03490-5 Much of the Amazon rainforest was thought to be evergreen, but high-resolution satellite imagery reveals that many of its trees can remain leafless for longer than expected.

item.title: Injured locusts heal or are cannibalized depending on levels of a bacterial odour molecule
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03599-7 When migratory locusts are injured, an odorous chemical produced by bacteria living in or on their bodies activates the immune system, helping them to fight disease-causing agents. However, when a wound is large and the chemical becomes too concentrated, it attracts cannibalistic locusts.

item.title: Are you a budding science sleuth? Take our plagiarism quiz to test your skills
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03040-z Sleuths and publishers seize on ‘tortured phrases’ to detect research fraud. Sometimes they can raise a smile.

item.title: AI must be held accountable — value statements won’t protect human dignity
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03717-5 Technology companies can’t be the judges of their own regulatory compliance. Centuries of history explain why.

item.title: A grant to hand out more grants — and build a research area
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03689-6 A rapid microgrants scheme called the Field Building Accelerator aims to launch new scientific fields.

item.title: Quantum physics can prove where you are
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03378-4 Demonstrating your location to someone far away is surprisingly hard. Quantum correlations offer a way to do so without needing to trust any quantum hardware.

item.title: The right to do wrong
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03517-x An equal chance.

item.title: Widespread deciduousness reveals diverse Amazonian phenological strategies
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11284-y A basin-wide assessment of Amazonian deciduousness using high-resolution satellite observations shows a diverse range of phenological strategies across the Amazon rainforest, contrary to the prevailing view of Amazonian phenology.

item.title: Observation of tunable superradiant frequency combs
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11289-7 A transition from continuous to periodic pulsed superradiant emission in coupled spin–resonator systems is demonstrated, revealing connections to time crystals and enabling synchronized microwave and optical frequency combs.

item.title: Rethinking corporate climate targets for real-world transitions
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11100-7 Frameworks for corporate greenhouse gas reduction targets should place greater emphasis on systemic changes in business models, technologies and value chains; the scientific community has a role in developing robust, actionable frameworks for corporate decarbonization.

item.title: Analogue simulation of massive relativistic quantum fields in 2 + 1 dimensions
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11268-y Analogue simulation of massive relativistic quantum fields in 2 + 1 dimensions (two spatial dimensions and time) is realized using two coherently coupled spin components in a two-dimensional atomic Bose–Einstein condensate.

item.title: A glucose-powered artificial neuroimmune axis for metabolic control
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11251-7 NeuroAxis restores glucose tolerance, improves insulin sensitivity and normalizes glycaemic control, with therapeutic effects persisting after treatment cessation in rat models of type 1 and type 2 diabetes.

item.title: Conservation of the tumour microenvironment across organs and species
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11270-4 A pan-cancer single-cell analysis of the tumour microenvironment across 42 cancer types and across 2 species is described.

item.title: Quantum position verification with remote untrusted devices
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11247-3 A loophole-free Bell-test quantum protocol demonstrates secure, device-independent position verification, achieving up to 4.53-fold smaller localization volumes than classical methods and enabling tamper-resistant location-based authentication.

item.title: Quantum resistance paradox of low-dimensional superfluids
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11294-w A defect-free unitary Fermi gas is used in a digitally programmable transport geometry to isolate geometric effects on superfluid dissipation and discover a paradox.

item.title: Fully integrated perovskite active polaritonic circuits
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11299-5 A fully integrated perovskite polaritonic circuit that brings the functionalities of fully integrated on-chip polaritonic systems simultaneously delivering room-temperature waveguide lasing, controllable optical routing and amplification together in a single-step-grown platform is shown.

item.title: TransA-MERFISH reveals divergent post-retinal direction-selective circuits
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11235-7 TransA-MERFISH combines anterograde trans-neuronal tracing and spatial transcriptomics and reveals distinct retinal on–off direction-selective ganglion cell-dependent and independent motion-selective pathways in superior colliculus, establishing a sensitive cell-type-resolved framework for wiring-diagram reconstruction in early visual processing.

item.title: Flat-band-induced integer doping and phase transition in monolayer graphene
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11254-4 An architecture comprising monolayer graphene doubly aligned to bulk and monolayer hBN on either side shows a gate-tunable global structural phase transition between two stacking configurations, accompanied by flat-band-induced integer doping.

item.title: Rainforest adaptation in late Homo erectus from southern China
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11155-6 Eight Homo erectus teeth from two caves in southern China reveal that the species persisted in closed rainforest ecosystems between 324 and 184 ka, challenging assumptions about their ecological preferences and behavioural limitations.

item.title: Bogong moths navigate with a light-dependent geomagnetic inclination compass
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11322-9 During their biannual migration, nocturnal Bogong moths (Agrotis infusa) rely on both a stellar and a geomagnetic compass for navigation, enabling them to maintain their migratory direction even if one of these cues is missing.

item.title: Why obesity affects men and women differently may be hiding in their fat
item.description: Scientists at the University of California, Riverside have uncovered a surprising reason why males and females may respond differently to obesity. In a study involving mice, researchers discovered that immune cells traditionally associated with allergies and asthma can either protect against obesity-related inflammation or contribute to harmful metabolic changes, depending on their type and biological sex.
